articles.title: The SUV That Could Change the Way America Drives
articles.standfirst: Hyundai just gave one of its most important SUVs a major makeover. I got my first look at the all-new Tucson in New York, and it is clear this is more than a styling update. The new generation is larger, more muscular and significantly more focused on technology, while Hyundai is also pushing the Tucson further into hybrid efficiency and weekend adventure.
articles.summary: Hyundai just gave one of its most important SUVs a major makeover. I got my first look at the all-new Tucson in New York, and it is clear this is more than a styling update. The new generation is larger, more muscular and significantly more focused on technology, while Hyundai is also pushing the Tucson further into hybrid efficiency and weekend adventure.
articles.body:
The global debut took place against the Manhattan skyline, an appropriate setting for a vehicle Hyundai describes as its “Boldest SUV.” The Tucson adopts the brand’s new “Art of Steel” design philosophy, with pronounced fenders, cleaner body surfaces and a wider stance that gives it a more substantial presence on the road.

The numbers confirm that this is a bigger SUV. The long-wheelbase version stretches 4,700 mm, or about 185 inches, making it 60 mm longer than the outgoing model. It is also 40 mm wider and 20 mm taller, while the wheelbase grows by 30 mm. Hyundai says those changes translate into additional interior space without losing the versatility that has made the Tucson one of its most important global products.

Since its introduction in 2004, the Tucson has accumulated more than 11.1 million global sales, making it Hyundai’s best-selling SUV worldwide. The United States represents roughly 20 percent of those cumulative sales, and hybrid demand has become particularly important. In 2025, hybrids represented 31 percent of Tucson sales in the U.S.

A hybrid that focuses on efficiency and performance

The new Tucson’s biggest mechanical story is Hyundai’s next-generation hybrid system. The North American hybrid targets up to 42 mpg with front-wheel drive and 17-inch wheels, while producing 233 horsepower. Hyundai quotes a 0-60 mph time of 8.5 seconds.

The idea is not simply to maximize fuel economy. Hyundai says the new system is designed to balance efficiency with driving performance, and the Tucson HEV also introduces E-Traction technology to improve grip and stability when cornering.

There is also a Plug-in Hybrid version in select markets, combining a 1.6-liter turbocharged engine with an electric motor for a total 292 PS and an estimated 81 kilometers, or about 50 miles, of electric range. A 7.2-kW onboard charger allows charging at home or public stations.

For buyers who prefer a conventional gasoline powertrain, the new Tucson will also offer a 1.6-liter turbocharged engine producing 184 horsepower in the U.S. specification.

The cabin gets a technology makeover

Inside, Hyundai has moved away from the traditional SUV dashboard and created a more open, furniture-inspired cabin. The instrument panel uses a two-layer design, while tactile controls remain below the central display for functions such as climate and audio.

That decision caught my attention because Hyundai is trying to solve one of the biggest problems with increasingly digital interiors: putting everything behind a touchscreen. The new Tucson combines physical controls with larger displays, including a 17-inch or 12.9-inch center screen depending on configuration and a 9.9-inch display positioned above the steering column.

The infotainment system is also new. Pleos Connect is based on Android Automotive OS and is designed to evolve through over-the-air updates. At the center of the experience is Gleo AI, Hyundai’s in-car conversational assistant.

Instead of searching through menus, drivers can use natural language to make requests. Hyundai’s example is asking the system to find a hiking trailhead with parking within 30 minutes . The goal is to make the technology feel more like an assistant and less like another screen to operate.

The cabin also gets practical upgrades, including dual 15-watt wireless charging pads, 100-watt USB-C charging and additional storage. The longer body provides up to 1,064 mm of rear legroom, while cargo capacity reaches 41.7 cubic feet under SAE measurements.

Tucson XRT PRO takes the SUV off the pavement

Hyundai is also expanding the Tucson’s personality with the XRT PRO, a version designed specifically for buyers who want more capability away from the pavement.

The XRT PRO features all-wheel drive, all-terrain tires, increased ground clearance and front recovery hooks. Ground clearance rises to 210 mm, approximately 30 mm more than the standard Tucson.

The biggest technology addition is Smart Terrain Assist, Hyundai’s first system of its kind. It evaluates terrain difficulty, traction and wheel slip and provides the driver with visual guidance. Target Speed Control can also manage acceleration and braking at low speeds on challenging terrain.

There is a Ground View Monitor for better visibility around the vehicle, Memory Reversing Assist that can help with steering while backing through narrow spaces, and Trailer Reverse Assist for easier maneuvering when towing.

For North American HEV models, towing capacity reaches 3,000 pounds, a significant increase over the previous generation.

A more comfortable place to spend time

Hyundai has also put considerable attention into making the Tucson a more comfortable vehicle for everyday use.

The interior incorporates softer surfaces and what Hyundai calls a more “furnished” approach to the cabin. Available features include Ergo Motion Seats with pneumatic lumbar and bolster massage, while a Relaxation Comfort Seat allows the passenger to recline at the touch of a button when the vehicle is parked.

The company has also developed a Multi-Air Mode system that distributes climate-controlled air through multiple vents and the floor rather than directing a strong stream of air directly at occupants.

Safety technology gets a significant upgrade as well. The Tucson can monitor driver eye activity and drowsiness, detect children or pets left inside the vehicle and provide navigation-linked assistance for curves, intersections and other road conditions.

Hyundai sees the Tucson as the beginning of something bigger

For José Muñoz , Hyundai Motor Company’s President and CEO, the new Tucson represents more than another model update. It is part of a much larger product strategy.

“Millions of families around the world count on the Hyundai TUCSON, and this is the best one we have ever built,” Muñoz said. “Its combination of bold design, generous cabin space, seamless infotainment, and available hybrid efficiency sets a new standard for what customers should expect in this segment.”

Muñoz also pointed to Hyundai’s broader product offensive, which calls for more than 100 new and refreshed vehicles globally by 2030, including 58 in North America.

That makes the Tucson an important vehicle to watch. Hyundai is using one of its best-known nameplates to bring together several of the trends defining the next generation of SUVs: hybrid efficiency, larger digital interfaces, conversational AI, increased interior comfort and more capable off-road technology.

The new Tucson will launch first in Korea later this year, with North America, Europe and other global markets following in 2027.

articles.title: From the Racetrack to Your Driveway: How Racing Technology Shapes Everyday Cars
articles.standfirst: There is something fascinating about standing next to a race car at Petit Le Mans and realizing that the technology being pushed to its limits on the track does not necessarily stay there.
articles.summary: There is something fascinating about standing next to a race car at Petit Le Mans and realizing that the technology being pushed to its limits on the track does not necessarily stay there.
articles.body:
At Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta, the Motul Petit Le Mans puts some of the fastest and most technologically advanced racing machines in the United States through a 10-hour endurance test. But at the Brembo stand, another side of motorsport technology comes into focus: racing is not only about developing technology to win races. It can also serve as a laboratory for the cars people drive every day.

Braking systems are one of the clearest examples.

When watching a race, the attention naturally goes to acceleration, top speed and overtaking. But going fast also means knowing how to slow down — precisely, repeatedly and consistently.

During an endurance race such as Petit Le Mans, where cars compete for 10 hours, braking systems have to withstand enormous amounts of heat, stress and repeated use.

The racetrack becomes a giant testing laboratory.

Brembo has spent decades developing braking systems for motorsport, including Formula 1, the FIA World Endurance Championship and MotoGP. Many technologies developed or refined for racing have eventually made their way into production vehicles, bringing racing experience to performance and safety on the road.

A clear example is the monoblock brake caliper.

Brembo developed its first monoblock caliper in 1987, with the technology making its Formula 1 debut the following year. Less than a decade later, it reached a production road car with the Porsche Boxster.

A solution created to meet the extreme demands of racing had made its way into a car that could leave a dealership and be driven on public roads.

The same philosophy can be seen in other braking technologies.

Carbon-based braking systems were originally developed to withstand the extreme conditions of motorsport. The challenge was then to adapt some of those characteristics for road cars, where brakes have to operate effectively at much lower temperatures and under very different conditions.

That development helped bring technologies such as carbon-ceramic brake discs to high-performance production vehicles.

And perhaps that is one of the most interesting things about an event like Petit Le Mans.

The technology surrounding these race cars can seem completely disconnected from everyday driving. The materials, demands and operating conditions are extreme. But the process behind them is relatively simple: develop, test, learn, improve — and, when possible, bring that knowledge to the vehicles people drive every day.

It is a philosophy the automotive industry has followed for decades.

Motorsport gives engineers an environment where components can be pushed far beyond the conditions they would normally experience on public roads. Every lap generates data. Every race can expose a weakness. Every improvement has to be ready for the next challenge.

In endurance racing, that philosophy becomes even more important.

Performance alone is not enough. Components must maintain their performance and reliability for hours. That is why championships such as IMSA and the FIA World Endurance Championship can also serve as testing grounds for new automotive technologies.

Watching a prototype race car fly through Road Atlanta, it is easy to think of it as a machine completely disconnected from the vehicles parked outside the circuit.

But there is a connection.

The next time a driver presses the brake pedal, the technology behind that action may have roots in decades of research and development that began in a very different environment: a racetrack, where engineers were looking for another tenth of a second.

That is one of the most fascinating aspects of motorsport.

The race ends. The technology continues.

articles.title: Henry Ford, American industrialist and business magnate: "You can't build a reputation on what you are going to do"
articles.standfirst: Ford believed promises mean little until they are backed up by consistent action
articles.summary: Ford believed promises mean little until they are backed up by consistent action
articles.body:
There is always another plan to talk about. A business will be launched once the timing is right. A difficult project will begin next month. A career change is coming soon.

Someone will finally follow through on the promise they have been making for weeks. Then there is the much harder part: actually doing it.

“You can’t build a reputation on what you are going to do,” Henry Ford once said. The line is short, but it exposes a gap that appears everywhere from business and sport to careers and personal relationships.

Intentions can sound impressive, yet they provide almost no evidence of what somebody can actually deliver. Reputation starts forming when promises are replaced by results.

People remember what happened

Planning has an obvious purpose. Almost every significant achievement begins with an idea, a target and some understanding of how to reach it.

The mistake is treating preparation as though it carries the same weight as execution.

A company can announce an ambitious product, but customers ultimately judge what reaches the market. An employee can promise improvement, but colleagues notice whether deadlines are actually met.

An athlete can talk about becoming fitter or more disciplined, but performance eventually provides the answer. That is what gives Ford’s observation its staying power.

Reputation is built from evidence accumulated over time. Each completed commitment adds something to it, while repeated promises without action gradually weaken it.

Words can introduce an expectation. Actions decide whether anyone believes the next one.

Reliability usually built in small moments

The strongest reputations are rarely created by one spectacular achievement.

They're more often constructed through ordinary consistency, such as arriving prepared, doing what was agreed, admitting mistakes and correcting them without needing to be chased.

That can feel less exciting than talking about a huge ambition, but it is far more persuasive.

Someone who repeatedly delivers eventually needs fewer explanations because their record begins speaking on their behalf.

The opposite is also true. Continually promising that things will be different can eventually make even sincere intentions difficult for others to trust.

Ford ’s quote therefore carries a lesson about patience as much as productivity.

Changing your reputation starts with behavior

The principle can also be encouraging for anyone trying to recover from a poor reputation.

People don't have to remain defined permanently by previous failures, but convincing others that change has happened usually requires more than saying so.

The most powerful response is sustained evidence. Do the work. Keep the commitment. Repeat the behavior long enough that the old perception no longer fits what people are seeing.

Recognition may not arrive immediately, and that can be frustrating. Reputation often changes more slowly than behavior. That doesn't make the effort pointless.

Ford ’s message is ultimately about closing the distance between intention and action. Ambition can point toward the person someone hopes to become, but reputation belongs to the person their actions have already revealed.
